newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Horlick pleads case, war of words continues.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Horlick pleads case, war of words continues.

text.p: Defiant and outspoken fund manager Nicola Horlick arrived in Frankfurt on Friday to plead for her job with top managers of Deutsche Bank, the parent of the fund management company from which she had been suspended.

The mother of five arrived in Germany's financial capital charging she had been penalised on the basis of hearsay and declaring: "That is appalling. I am sorry, I am not going to be treated like this."

But Deutsche said the high-flyer reputed to have been earning one million pounds ($1.67 million) a year at London-based Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, had no appointment. It looked as if the doors to the bank's top executives would remain firmly shut after Deutsche Morgan Grenfell hinted that such a meeting was highly unlikely.
But on her arrival at Deutsche's headquarters, Horlick, dubbed "superwoman" by the British media did meet an unnamed official, however.
Horlick, 35, flew to Frankfurt after announcing late on Thursday that she had resigned.

At Frankfurt airport, Horlick, 35, made two phone calls to London and was told that she would not be given a meeting with Deutsche executives. She then walked to a check-in to desk to book a flight back to London for later on Friday.
"I'm trying to get my job back. I'm here to see members of the Deutsche Bank management board. This is one individual against a huge organisation," Horlick told reporters.

As the war of words between the two sides hotted up, Horlick said: "There has been a very large misunderstanding. They (MGAM) should have asked me, they decided to suspend me on the basis of hearsay."
Earlier, she was quoted as saying that allegations she was attempting to move to a competitor firm were "absolutely untrue" and that the charges against her were "trumped up."
MGAM chief executive Robert Smith told staff in an internal memo that Horlick had been suspended two days earlier for "soliciting senior colleagues to join a competitor."
Horlick repeated her assertion that she had been "constructively dismissed" by the asset management company and this had forced her resignation.

Her advisers said that if her pleas go unheeded, Horlick plans to take legal action against MGAM for unfair dismissal and will also claim money which she says is due to her from the firm. A Deutsche Morgan Grenfell spokesman said in London that no legal action had been started as yet.
Horlick's resignation came as it emerged she had been offered and accepted the position of managing director of MGAM just days before her suspension.
MGAM's Smith told staff that the firm stands by its actions and wants to develop what he termed its "great" business.
"No one individual is bigger than the institution," Smith told his staff.
"We are standing by our actions and we are completely satisfied that we have acted properly throughout," Smith said.

In a telephone interview with Reuters, Smith said he did not think the affair would damage MGAM's business -- "I don't think so, it's not very pretty reading, of course, and no one enjoys reading about themselves the way we're being described but I don't think it will do lasting damage."
Recent developments are said by industry sources to have revived concerns among MGAM's pension fund clients first raised by the Peter Young affair last year.

"Horlick, a solid team and a good investment performance had given MGAM a stay of execution...But there seem to be several disgruntled staff around which is not good. They'll be facing a very difficult time from clients," said one fund consultant.

"They would have to decide where to put the money and finding another fund manager would take a number of weeks rather than days. That and the deterrent of the costs involved would slow any potential loss of business," he added.
